chapters.title: Chapter 3: Hedging a Mutual Fund or Diversified Portfolio with Nifty Options

lessons.title: You Cannot Buy Options on Your Mutual Fund: The Index Proxy Solution

children.text: Most Indian investors do not own twenty individual stocks. They own mutual funds, fed by SIPs that have run into tens of thousands of crores every month. So here is the awkward truth for anyone who has read this far: there is no such thing as a put option on the Parag Parikh Flexi Cap Fund or the HDFC Mid-Cap Opportunities Fund. Mutual fund units have no exchange-traded options at all. You cannot insure the exact thing you own. What you can do is insure something that behaves like it, and that is what this chapter is about.

body.text: When you hedge a mutual fund portfolio with index options, you are not hedging your funds. You are hedging the part of your funds that moves with the index. The quality of your hedge depends entirely on how much your portfolio looks like that index.

children.text: What You Can Actually Buy Options On

markDefs.definition: Hedging a position using a different instrument whose price tends to move in the same direction, because no derivative exists on the position itself.

children.text: Options in India exist only on a short list of underlyings: a little over 200 F&O-eligible stocks and a handful of indices. No mutual fund and no ETF has its own options. So a fund investor has one realistic route:
proxy hedging
, using options on an index that the portfolio broadly tracks.

body.caption: Index options available to Indian investors (check NSE and BSE for current contract details)

cells: Deep, across many strikes and several months out. The default hedging tool
The largest, most liquid banking stocks
Banks, NBFCs, insurers and other financial companies
A concentrated basket of liquid midcap stocks
Thin, with wide bid-ask spreads on many strikes
The 50 companies ranked just below the Nifty 50

body.text: In practice, almost every retail portfolio hedge in India comes down to Nifty 50 options, with Nifty Bank as an occasional second tool. The other contracts exist, but thin trading means a hedger can lose a noticeable slice of the premium just to the gap between buying and selling prices.

children.text: How Well Does the Proxy Fit Your Fund?

A Nifty put pays out on what the Nifty does. Your portfolio loses what your funds do. The closer those two are, the better the hedge. Fund categories give a quick first read, because SEBI's categorisation rules decide what each type of fund is allowed to hold.

body.caption: How well index options can hedge common mutual fund categories

cells: Holds the same stocks in the same weights, apart from small tracking differences
At least 80% in the top 100 companies, with heavy overlap with the Nifty 50
Nifty Bank or Nifty Financial Services
Concentrated in the same sector the index tracks
Flexi cap or multi cap fund
A mix of large, mid and small caps that can behave quite differently from the Nifty
Usually diversified like a flexi cap fund. The three-year lock-in also makes a hedge more attractive than selling
Midcaps often fall harder than the Nifty in corrections
Small caps can move very differently and fall far more sharply
Sector funds such as IT or pharma
Driven by sector-specific factors the Nifty only partly reflects
Driven by foreign markets and the rupee, not the Nifty
Balanced advantage or equity savings funds
These funds already adjust their net equity exposure, often using derivatives themselves

body.title: Pick the proxy
body.question: Nisha, a 36-year-old consultant in Gurugram, holds ₹15 lakh in a banking and financial services sector fund and nothing else in equity. Which index options would give her the closest proxy hedge?
options: Nifty Bank or Nifty Financial Services
body.explanation: Her fund is concentrated in banks and financial companies, which is exactly what Nifty Bank and Nifty Financial Services track. The Nifty 50 includes large bank stocks but also IT, energy, consumer and other sectors that her fund does not own, so it would be a looser fit.

children.text: Breaking a Real Portfolio Into Hedgeable Pieces

Rohan, 47, is a finance controller at a manufacturing company in Pune. His ₹25 lakh equity portfolio is typical of an experienced SIP investor: a core index fund, a couple of active funds and a US fund he added in 2021. Before thinking about lots or strikes, he sorts each holding by how well the Nifty 50 can stand in for it.

body.caption: Rohan's portfolio sorted by how well Nifty 50 options can hedge it

stats.label: Strong or good fit
stats.context: A Nifty hedge will track these closely

stats.label: Partial or weak fit
stats.context: Moves with the Nifty, but not one for one

stats.label: No fit
stats.context: A Nifty hedge does nothing for the US fund

children.text: This simple sort already tells Rohan three useful things. Half his portfolio can be hedged with confidence. Another 40% can be hedged, but the hedge will over- or under-compensate depending on how his flexi cap and mid cap funds behave compared with the Nifty. And 10% sits completely outside any Indian index hedge. The next lesson turns "partial" into a number, using beta.

body.title: Sort a portfolio
body.prompt: Anjali holds ₹6 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund, ₹4 lakh in a large cap fund, ₹5 lakh in a small cap fund and ₹3 lakh in a Nasdaq 100 fund of funds. Using the fit table above, how many rupees of her portfolio have a strong or good fit with Nifty 50 options?
body.explanation: Strong fit: ₹6 lakh (Nifty 50 index fund). Good fit: ₹4 lakh (large cap fund). Total ₹10,00,000, which is about 56% of her ₹18 lakh. The small cap fund is a weak fit and the Nasdaq fund has no fit at all.

children.text: Look Through the Label: Check What Your Fund Really Holds

Category names are a starting point, not the answer. Two flexi cap funds can be completely different: one may hold 75% large caps and look a lot like the Nifty, another may hold 40% mid and small caps plus a slice of foreign stocks. Every fund publishes a monthly factsheet and full portfolio disclosure. Four numbers from it tell you most of what you need.
Market cap split:
the percentage in large, mid and small caps. The higher the large cap share, the better a Nifty proxy fits.
Top holdings and sector weights:
compare them with the Nifty 50's. A fund heavy in sectors the Nifty underweights will drift away from it.
Cash and foreign holdings:
cash and overseas stocks will not fall with the Nifty, so a fund with 10% cash needs a slightly smaller hedge.
Beta, if the factsheet reports it:
many factsheets show the fund's beta against its benchmark. You will use this in the next lesson.

body.text: Check which benchmark the factsheet's beta is measured against. Many flexi cap and mid cap funds report beta against a broad index such as the Nifty 500 or Nifty Midcap 150, not the Nifty 50. A beta of 0.9 against the Nifty 500 does not mean 0.9 against the Nifty 50. For hedging with Nifty 50 options, you need the relationship to the Nifty 50 specifically.

body.title: Name the method
body.textWithBlank: Using Nifty 50 options to protect a flexi cap mutual fund, because no options exist on the fund itself, is an example of ___ hedging.
body.explanation: Proxy hedging, sometimes called cross hedging, uses a related instrument when no derivative exists on what you actually own. It always leaves some mismatch, known as basis risk.

children.text: Why Hedge Instead of Just Redeeming?

body.title: Redeeming funds vs hedging them with index puts

columns.label: Redeem and move to debt
points: Removes the risk completely, with no basis mismatch
Can trigger capital gains tax on years of accumulated gains
May attract exit load if units are recent, commonly 1% within a year
ELSS units still in lock-in cannot be redeemed at all
Hard to decide when to get back in, and easy to miss the recovery

columns.label: Stay invested and hedge with index puts
points: Keeps units, SIPs and tax position untouched
Cost is limited to the premium and transaction charges
Protection is only as good as the proxy fit
Requires an F&O-enabled trading account and enough capital for full lots
Needs monitoring and rolling, which many investors find harder than expected

body.title: The small cap and IT investor
body.scenario: Farhan, 44, runs a travel agency in Kolkata. His ₹30 lakh equity portfolio is ₹14 lakh in two small cap funds, ₹10 lakh in a technology sector fund and ₹6 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund. After reading about protective puts, he wants to buy Nifty puts covering the full ₹30 lakh ahead of a period he expects to be volatile.
body.prompt: How well would a Nifty 50 put hedge protect Farhan's portfolio? What would you point out to him before he places the order?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Only ₹6 lakh, 20% of his portfolio, is a strong fit. The small cap funds (47%) and the tech fund (33%) are weak fits.
2. In a broad correction, small caps have often fallen much harder than the Nifty. A put that pays out on, say, a 12% Nifty fall may leave most of a 25% small cap fall unprotected.
3. The reverse can also happen. A sector-specific shock to IT, such as a US tech slowdown, can hit his tech fund hard while the Nifty barely moves, and the Nifty put pays nothing.
4. Hedging the full ₹30 lakh with Nifty puts would over-hedge the index-like part and under-protect the rest. He could pay a large premium and still suffer large losses.
5. Better questions first: is the portfolio's concentration in small caps and one sector a deliberate choice he is comfortable with? If the underlying worry is too much risk, rebalancing towards large caps or debt addresses it directly. If he still wants a hedge, it should be sized carefully using beta, which the next lesson covers, with a clear understanding that it is only a partial fix.
The lesson: an index hedge cannot repair a portfolio that looks nothing like the index.

body.title: What about selling Nifty futures instead of buying puts?

children.text: Selling Nifty futures is another proxy hedge. A short future gains one point for every point the Nifty falls, so it offsets losses from the very first rupee, with no premium to pay. The catch is symmetry: it also loses one point for every point the Nifty rises, so a fully futures-hedged portfolio gives up all its upside too. It also needs margin and daily mark-to-market cash settlement, which means you may have to add money during a rally.

For an investor who wants to stay invested for the upside and simply cap the downside, puts fit the goal better. Futures suit someone who wants to temporarily neutralise market exposure altogether, which is closer to selling. The Futures & Derivatives Explained course covers futures in depth.

body.title: Map your own portfolio to a proxy
steps: List every equity fund you hold with its current value, from your CAS statement or your investment app.
Note each fund's SEBI category and classify its fit with the Nifty 50 using the table in this lesson.
Open the latest factsheet for every partial-fit fund and note its large, mid and small cap split and cash holding.
Add up the rupee value in strong or good fit, partial fit and no fit.
Decide which part of the portfolio a Nifty hedge is actually meant to protect, before thinking about lots or strikes.

cards.definition: Hedging with a related instrument, such as Nifty options, when no derivative exists on the holding itself.
The risk that the hedged holding and the hedging instrument move differently, leaving losses unprotected or over-compensated.
How closely a fund's movements track the index used to hedge it. Strongest for index and large cap funds.
Checking a fund's actual holdings, market cap split and cash in its factsheet rather than relying on its category label.
NSE's index option contract on liquid midcaps. A closer proxy for mid cap funds, but thinly traded.
Selling index futures to offset losses. No premium, but it also gives up the upside and requires margin.

points: Mutual funds and ETFs have no options of their own. Fund investors hedge through index options as a proxy.
Nifty 50 options are the only index options with deep liquidity across strikes and expiries. Most retail hedges use them.
Index and large cap funds fit a Nifty hedge well. Flexi, multi and mid cap funds fit partially. Small cap, sector and international funds fit poorly or not at all.
Sort your portfolio by fit before sizing any hedge, and look through fund labels to their actual holdings.
Hedging lets you stay invested without triggering tax, exit loads or lock-in problems, but protection is only as good as the proxy.
An index hedge cannot fix a portfolio that looks nothing like the index.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Fund names are mentioned only as examples of fund categories, not as recommendations. Contract availability and liquidity on NSE and BSE change over time. Investor portfolios are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before hedging or rebalancing your portfolio.
